strengths: Clear identification and validation of perception as the bottleneck in abstract visual reasoning, with compelling empirical evidence across 17 MLLMs
Comprehensive benchmark design with systematic coverage of five core perceptual dimensions grounded in cognitive science, addressing a gap in existing evaluations
Well-documented data collection and quality control pipeline with 12 trained annotators ensuring high-quality benchmark construction
Extensive experimental evaluation showing perceptual supervision significantly improves performance (43.7% vs 20.9% baseline) without architectural changes
Automated synthesis framework (PRS) provides a scalable approach to generating training data with intermediate supervision, demonstrated to be more effective than reasoning-only approaches
Rigorous demonstration that scaling approaches and CoT prompting alone cannot solve AVR tasks without addressing perception
weaknesses: Critical experimental gap: ablation study validating perceptual supervision (Table 4) conducted only on synthetic data subset, not on actual VisuRiddles benchmark—domain transfer not demonstrated

Limited conceptual novelty: benchmark primarily consolidates existing civil service exam problems; five dimensions are established in prior cognitive science work; RAVEN/Sudoku are incorporated existing benchmarks
Insufficient analysis of synthetic-to-real domain gap: models trained on rule-based synthetic data with explicit annotations; unclear how perceptual descriptions help on unannotated real data
Incomplete failure analysis: only one case study provided; 'Other' category shows unexpected negative improvements with more data (-1.9% to -0.4%) left unexplained; no systematic error breakdown

Benchmark size concerns: 1000 total samples (800 in basic categories), modest for comprehensive evaluation; 'Other' category poorly defined; perfectly balanced answer distributions may not reflect natural difficulty

Underspecified technical details: how are 'plausible distractors' generated; justification for 34 sub-rules unclear; no comparison with alternative supervision strategies or human-written descriptions
Limited generalization evidence: all evaluated models are VLMs; no cross-dataset evaluation on other benchmarks; applicability to other visual reasoning tasks unclear

Claim validation incomplete: while perceptual supervision helps, alternative explanations not ruled out (e.g., regularization effects, data volume, model capacity); causality not definitively established

strengths: Well-motivated investigation of MLLM limitations in abstract visual reasoning with a clear diagnostic insight via Figure 1
Carefully constructed benchmark (VisuRiddles) with rigorous curation pipeline, grounding in cognitive science, and balanced annotation
Systematic synthetic data generation framework (PRS) with modular design, 34 sub-rules, and structured perceptual annotations
Comprehensive evaluation of 17 models with multiple experimental angles (main results, ablations, visualizations) showing perception substantially improves accuracy
Strong empirical improvements across most categories, particularly on structured tasks (Sudoku, RAVEN)
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and thorough related work section
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core insight that perception bottlenecks reasoning is intuitive; intermediate supervision and synthetic data are established techniques
Potential circular evaluation: PRS extracts patterns from same exam sources as VisuRiddles benchmark, creating risk of pattern overlap and test contamination; no quantitative analysis of this overlap
Suspicious experimental results suggest pattern matching rather than genuine learning: Sudoku accuracy jumps from 0% to 60%, RAVEN from 14% to 95%; baseline 0% on Sudoku unexplained

Synthetic data deliberately kept tractable rather than replicating real-world difficulty, limiting evidence of genuine perceptual learning; negative transfer in 'Other' category (Table 5) contradicts main claims
Benchmark limitations: only 1,000 samples (small by modern standards), imbalanced categories (69-250 samples each), single source with potential linguistic/cultural bias, no cross-dataset validation

Unclear what is actually learned: perceptual descriptions might simply provide explicit reasoning scaffolding rather than teaching visual perception; no probing analysis to distinguish these mechanisms

Limited generalization evidence: all evaluation confined to VisuRiddles; no transfer to other visual reasoning tasks or zero-shot performance; unclear if improvements are benchmark-specific or general
Insufficient technical details: perceptual description format vague, rendering engine details missing, single learning rate for all experiments, no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Weak statistical rigor: no error bars, significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement reported; human baseline mentioned but not systematically evaluated; single experimental run
Incomplete analysis of failure modes and generalization boundaries beyond single case study in Figure 4

strengths: Clear problem identification with strong motivation: effectively demonstrates that MLLMs fail at AVR due to perception limitations, not reasoning, supported by compelling evidence (Figure 1, Table 4 with +32.5% improvement from perceptual descriptions)

Comprehensive and well-structured benchmark: VisuRiddles spans five cognitively-grounded dimensions plus high-level reasoning tasks, with rigorous quality control (12 annotators, multi-pass review), balanced answer distributions, and systematic consolidation

Novel intermediate supervision approach: PRS innovatively generates both synthetic images and fine-grained perceptual descriptions enabling supervision over the perception-to-reasoning pipeline, beyond standard data generation

Extensive experimental validation: 17 MLLMs evaluated with well-designed ablations (Table 4: visual vs. perceptual inputs), progressive data scaling (Table 5), and systematic analysis showing reasoning enhancements (CoT, thinking modes) provide limited benefits

Strong empirical evidence for main claim: Multiple lines of converging evidence (perception bottleneck hypothesis validated through visual vs. perceptual input comparison, case studies showing inference-time scaling failures, and consistent improvements with synthetic data)
Practical community value: Delivers 1,000-question benchmark, 80k+ synthetic samples with perceptual annotations, and automated synthesis framework with 34 sub-rules, 8 layouts, and 10k icons
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figures 1 and 4 clearly communicate key insights; writing is generally well-organized and accessible
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty in benchmark design: Five perceptual dimensions are explicitly drawn from existing cognitive science (refs 63-66); RAVEN and Sudoku are existing benchmarks. Contribution is primarily organizational rather than introducing novel task types or evaluation paradigms

Critical unresolved generalization concern: Massive performance gap between synthetic and real tasks (e.g., RAVEN: 95% on synthetic vs. ~13% on real from Table 3; 82 percentage point gap) is neither adequately explained nor analyzed. Raises questions whether training actually improves perception or just learns synthetic task patterns

Inadequate error analysis and diagnostic evaluation: Missing systematic breakdown of failure modes across five dimensions, no ablations identifying which perceptual description components matter most, no feature importance analysis (which visual attributes most impact performance), and no explanation for unexpectedly low human performance (63%)

Insufficient validation of synthetic data quality: No inter-annotator agreement or reliability metrics reported; translations from Chinese civil service exams without discussion of potential artifacts; limited analysis of whether synthetic descriptions accurately reflect image content or whether perceptual descriptions match human processes

Unexplained negative transfer and inconsistencies: Performance degradation in 'Other' category (-2.6%) is mentioned but not analyzed; the dramatic performance jump on RAVEN/Sudoku (14%→95%, 0%→60%) suggests potential overfitting to synthetic rules rather than learning generalizable perception

Insufficient ablations and comparisons: No ablations on importance of different perceptual description types; no comparison with alternative synthetic data generation strategies; no evaluation on other AVR benchmarks (PGM, ConceptARC, etc.) to validate generalization; missing comparison with other perception-enhancement approaches (vision pre-training, contrastive learning)

Design-synthetic task mismatch undermines transfer claims: Paper explicitly states synthetic tasks are 'deliberately kept tractable' rather than replicating real-world difficulty. This deliberate simplification contradicts the goal of improving performance on complex real AVR tasks

Incomplete reproducibility documentation: Exact perceptual description format not fully specified; PRS implementation details sparse; no discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity; promised code/data unavailable for review; no reporting of error bars, confidence intervals, or number of training runs

Missing cross-domain evaluation: No evaluation on other visual reasoning benchmarks or domains to establish generalization beyond VisuRiddles; unclear whether improvements transfer to other AVR tasks; no evidence this approach helps with visual reasoning more broadly

Insufficient analysis of human baseline: Only 63% human accuracy reported for tasks claimed to be 'relatively easy for humans.' This discrepancy is not explained—are task instructions unclear, or is benchmark genuinely harder than claimed?

strengths: Clear problem identification with compelling evidence (Figure 1b) that structured perceptual descriptions enable models to solve problems they fail on with raw images
Comprehensive benchmark with 1,000 carefully curated AVR problems from real exams, covering 8 diverse reasoning categories with structured quality control
Strong ablation studies (Tables 3-4) convincingly demonstrate perception bottleneck: GPT-4o improves from 27.6% to 60.1%, Qwen2.5VL from 30.9% to 73.6% with descriptions
Well-designed synthesizer that automatically generates 20K+ training instances with aligned perceptual descriptions across modular rule categories
Extensive empirical evaluation across 17+ models (11 open-source, 6 commercial) with clear performance improvements
Good visualization and interpretability (Figures 4-5) illustrating failure modes and the model's rethinking phenomenon
Planned public release of benchmark and code will benefit the community
weaknesses: Critical comparison fairness issue: Only PAVR is fine-tuned on synthetic data; all baselines use zero-shot/CoT. Unclear whether improvements stem from perception-augmentation or domain-specific fine-tuning. Missing control: fine-tuning baselines on same synthetic data without perceptual descriptions

Limited generalization: Results on VisuLogic (30.6%) are only marginally better than some baselines (InternVL2.5-38B-RL: 31.1%), raising questions about whether gains are specific to VisuRiddles-style problems

Dataset scale and diversity constraints: Only 1,000 samples with single source (Chinese civil service exams); acknowledged in paper that rule design and icon library are restricted, limiting diversity of synthesized data

Technical novelty is limited: Two-stage SFT+RL approach is not novel; concurrent work on similar methods (R1-OneVision, Visual-RFT). Perceptual descriptions are orthogonal to the core insight about fine-grained perception

Incomplete disentanglement of perception vs. reasoning: Table 3 uses synthetically-generated data (simpler than real benchmark); no analysis of failure modes or cases where better perception doesn't enable correct reasoning
Statistical rigor lacking: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement reporting. Figure 5's 'rethinking' phenomenon observed but not quantified
Generalization not tested beyond AVR: Only evaluated on 2 AVR benchmarks; unclear if perception augmentation helps on other visual reasoning tasks
Large gap to human performance remains (46.8% vs. 63.0%), indicating PAVR still falls substantially short of human-level performance

strengths: Clear and well-motivated hypothesis with effective demonstration (Figure 1b) that perceptual descriptions substantially improve performance
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 17 MLLMs (both open-source and commercial), providing convincing evidence of widespread AVR weakness
Systematic ablation studies (Tables 3-4) effectively decomposing perception vs. reasoning contributions
Well-engineered VisuRiddles benchmark covering 8 reasoning categories with balanced answer distributions and structured construction pipeline
Thorough qualitative analysis including case studies (Figure 5) comparing different reasoning strategies and their failure modes
Thoughtfully designed two-stage synthesizer producing interpretable training data with structured perceptual annotations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: The core insight that perception matters is intuitive; the SFT+RL approach is straightforward; GRPO is borrowed from prior work

Core claim ('perception is primary bottleneck') not definitively validated: Improvements from descriptions could stem from reduced visual processing burden or hybrid perception-reasoning benefits rather than proving perception is primary
Serious generalization concerns: PAVR achieves only 30.6% on VisuLogic vs. 46.8% on VisuRiddles, markedly underperforming and suggesting limited applicability beyond the benchmark

Potential methodological issues: (1) Circular evaluation—synthesized training data from rule-based generation while benchmark from real exams; (2) Gemini generates CoT labels for training data then compared against Gemini in evaluation; (3) PAVR fine-tuned while baselines unadjusted, unfair comparison
Benchmark construction under-documented: Only 1000 samples (small scale), unclear reduction process from 1,275 to 1,000, no inter-annotator agreement reported, vague definition of 'real-world data'
Synthesizer produces lower-difficulty data than real riddles (acknowledged), yet impact on generalization to harder problems is unexplored
Weak performance on VisuLogic (30.6%) only marginally beats InternVL2.5-38B-RL (31.1%), undermining claims of approach's broad applicability
No statistical rigor: Missing confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests; small benchmark size reduces statistical power

Incomplete analysis: Sudoku near-0% across models unexplained; no systematic error categorization; 'rethink' phenomenon interesting but not analyzed; 16.2% gap to human performance (63%) understates remaining challenges
Reproducibility concerns: Code/datasets stated as 'will be released' with no links provided; GRPO hyperparameters under-specified; requires 8 A800 GPUs limiting accessibility

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement with compelling empirical evidence (Table 3) that fine-grained perception is a bottleneck for MLLMs on AVR tasks

Comprehensive resource contributions: VisuRiddles benchmark (1000 questions across 8 reasoning types) derived from real-world exams, and a synthesizer for generating training data with structured perceptual descriptions
Thorough experimental evaluation across 23 models with detailed ablation studies (Tables 3-4) that convincingly isolate the contribution of perception vs. reasoning
Clear findings that standard techniques (model scaling, CoT prompting) are insufficient for AVR, providing useful negative results
Well-executed experimental design with careful quality control for benchmark curation and clear structured evaluation methodology
Effective visualizations and writing that clearly communicate the main insights, particularly Figure 5's comparison of reasoning strategies
Practical two-stage training paradigm (SFT + GRPO) that progressively enhances both perception and reasoning abilities
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: applies existing techniques (SFT + GRPO from DeepSeek-R1) without proposing new algorithms or architectures
Significant generalization concerns: PAVR achieves 30.6% on VisuLogic benchmark vs. 31.1% for InternVL2.5-38B-RL, undermining claims of generalizability across AVR tasks

Fundamental train-test mismatch: synthesized riddles are deliberately kept easier than real-world problems (acknowledged in Section 3.2), creating a distribution gap that may limit practical effectiveness
Relatively small benchmark scale (1000 total questions, with only 100 each for RAVEN/Sudoku) with limited human performance data (single point estimate without inter-annotator agreement details)
Incomplete comparative analysis: PAVR results compared against baselines without perceptual augmentation; lacks showing whether the SFT+GRPO recipe works on other base models
Limited failure case analysis and ablation on reward design choices; GRPO reward function minimally described with only Answer + Format rewards mentioned
Reproducibility concerns: relies on proprietary Gemini API for CoT generation; requires 8 A800 GPUs; unclear independence of generated RAVEN/Sudoku from model training data
Weak theoretical insights: primarily empirical without deep explanation of why perception is critical for abstract reasoning or what specific perceptual capabilities are learned
No statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, cross-validation, or variance analysis across random seeds
